 Blackhawks defenseman Bowen Byram now seeing specialist as injury saga continues
 Byram is not yet medically cleared to return from the upper-body injury that has sidelined him for three weeks, even though he has had a “day-to-day” designation the whole time.
 By  
 Ben Pope 
 [month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone] 
 Bowen Byram hasn’t played for the Blackhawks since Oct. 13.
 Michael Reaves/Getty Images
 SHARE 
 COPY LINK 
 Share
 CLOSE

 Facebook 
 Bluesky 
 Email 
 Reddit 
 Flipboard 
 Defenseman Bowen Byram is seeing a medical specialist whom the Blackhawks hope can help get him over the ‘‘last hurdle’’ in his recovery from an undisclosed upper-body injury, coach Jeff Blashill said Monday.
 It’s the latest development in a confusing story that initially seemed innocuous but now has stretched for three weeks. Byram missed his eighth consecutive game Monday and ninth out of 15 this season.
 In the meantime, the Hawks have forged on — not very successfully — without their biggest offseason trade acquisition, whom they believed would add much-needed star power to their young defensive corps.
 Byram’s poor performance in his first six appearances cast some doubt on that thinking, but he also was adjusting to new systems and teammates, getting little support and learning how to be a parent to newborn twin daughters at home.
 When he returns, it’s possible he’ll transform the Hawks for the better, both by bumping every other defenseman into more appropriate roles for their skills and by using his quickness and puck-moving ability to help the team transition from defense to offense. The Hawks haven’t been shy about attributing some of their struggles to his absence.
 None of this can be assessed, however, until Byram returns, and it’s unclear when that will be.
 He last played Oct. 13 against the Penguins and showed no visible signs of injury. He led the team with 24 minutes, 37 seconds of ice time and was on the ice to congratulate goalie Spencer Knight after the Hawks’ victory.
 When Byram wasn’t at the Hawks’ morning skate Oct. 15, Blashill said he was considered ‘‘day-to-day’’ with an upper-body injury. He has maintained that day-to-day designation ever since.
 Blashill has clarified it isn’t a concussion, which many fans initially speculated about because Byram was hit in the head with a puck during the game against the Penguins and dealt with concussion-related issues earlier in his career with the Avalanche. But Blashill hasn’t specified the exact injury.
 Byram resumed skating individually Oct. 23 and resumed practicing with the team — while wearing a gray non-contact jersey — the next day. He then traveled with the Hawks on their road trip last week to Detroit and Boston but ended up not playing in either game. He was seen in the press box in Boston.
 Byram wasn’t on the ice at all for the morning skate Monday in Chicago, after which Blashill said he hasn’t suffered a setback but isn’t yet medically cleared to play. That contradicted a report by Frank Seravalli on Chicago Sports Network’s pregame show Saturday.
 Blashill didn’t answer a question about whether Byram will travel with the Hawks on Tuesday for the start of their three-game road trip against the Panthers, Lightning and Hurricanes.
 During Byram’s absence, the Hawks have distributed their hardest minutes among four defensemen: Alex Vlasic, Artyom Levshunov, Wyatt Kaiser and Ian Cole. Each has averaged between 21:30 and 19:30 per game.
 Sam Rinzel has been sheltered as much as possible, and Ethan Del Mastro and Kevin Korchinski have rotated in and out of the lineup. Blashill described the group’s play as ‘‘up and down.’’
 ‘‘Certain guys have definitely grown,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘Vlasic had a tough one [Oct. 1] in Utah. Other than that, he’s been really good on a consistent basis.
 ‘‘You pretty much know what you’re getting every night with Cole. That’s a good feeling as a coach — to know when he goes out, you know what you’re getting. The last four or five games, Kaiser has been really good. [He] certainly still isn’t without a mistake, but that’s probably nobody.’’
 Levshunov, meanwhile, has been arguably the brightest spot of the unit, restoring faith that he might be able to develop into the elite top-pairing defenseman the Hawks drafted him to be. But even he is handicapped without Byram as a possible partner.
